name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 3 November 1983

clue.text: Discourage familiarity in far-flung fortress

blocks.note: a keep is the strongest tower of a castle
far-flung things lie a long way off

explanation.surface: A remote castle whose very remoteness puts off would-be friends.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold someone off socially, refusing closeness, is an idiom for discouraging familiarity.

clue.text: Will apple cider do for David's helpmeet?

indicators.note: the question asks whether the following words can be made to serve, that is reshaped into something else

blocks.note: taken as written: fifteen letters to rework

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a glass of cider is good enough for David's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do for' looks like 'suit', but every letter from 'apple' to 'for' is fodder. In Dickens's David Copperfield, Dora Spenlow becomes David's first wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A helpmeet is a wife or companion, and Dora was the wife of Dickens's hero David Copperfield.

clue.text: Send pioneers to Ireland and stop restlessness, perhaps

blocks.note: to settle a territory is to send colonists to it
Down is a county of Northern Ireland, standing for the place itself

explanation.surface: A colonial plan to calm unrest by planting settlers in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ireland' is not the whole island but one county in it, County Down.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle down is to become calm and stop fidgeting, an example of ending restlessness, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Look at cricket as prescribed by optician

definitions.note: describes the answer rather than defining it as a noun

blocks.note: to eye something is to look at it
a Test is an international cricket match

explanation.surface: An optician recommends watching cricket as therapy for the eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: An optician orders a sight examination to check vision before prescribing lenses.

clue.text: The island sounds heavenly

indicators.note: sounds tells us to go by how a word is said, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: the heavens are the sky above

explanation.surface: A Scottish island whose name rings out like paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: Skye is an island of the Scottish Hebrides; the answer is pronounced exactly like the word for the heavens.
explanation.definitionFit: Skye is a large island off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: Like the extravagance of the long-jump winner?

definitions.text: Like the extravagance of the long-jump winner?

blocks.note: surface reading: describing excess that knows no limit
setter's reading: the winning jump lands further than every other athlete's leap

explanation.surface: A champion jumper's lavish lifestyle is held up for comment.
explanation.walkthrough: A bound is a leap, so the winner's jump is literally past all the other jumps; the phrase also means excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means excessive or unrestrained, which describes extravagance; literally it puts the winning leap past every other jump.

clue.text: Don't buy a flag from the dustman

blocks.note: first meaning, read as an order: turn down the charity worker who sells paper flags on a flag day
second meaning: the worker who empties household bins

explanation.surface: Advice not to buy a charity flag when the dustman rattles the tin.
explanation.walkthrough: On flag days charities sold small paper flags in the street; the person with the tin is a collector, and 'refuse' is read as a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A dustman, in British usage, is the worker who collects household rubbish, also called refuse.

clue.text: Some light on hard-core restoration?

indicators.note: hard can mean rough or tough, treating the word next to it roughly so its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the four letters of core, reworked
a Very light is a coloured signal flare fired from a pistol

explanation.surface: Restoring something to its hard core, with a bit of lighting added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard-core' reads as one adjective but splits into an instruction and its fodder; 'on' puts the light after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Recovery is the act of getting something back to its former state, a synonym for restoration.

clue.text: Custodian in the ring

blocks.note: first meaning: a guardian or person in charge
second meaning: a guard ring worn to hold another ring on the finger

explanation.walkthrough: 'in the ring' suggests a boxing ring; the setter means a jeweller's guard ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A keeper looks after something, and is also the name for a small band worn to keep a wedding ring from slipping off.

clue.text: Current rising brings pact with United States, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints the words are only one possible arrangement of their letters

blocks.note: taken as written
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A rising political tide leads to a treaty with America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pact with United States' looks like the definition; it is the fodder, and 'Current rising' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: In mining, an upcast is the upward flow of air leaving a mine through its ventilation shaft.

clue.text: See them about four may be in the old market-place

indicators.note: may be says the word shown is only one of the forms its letters could take
about means around, so one word is wrapped round the other

blocks.note: the letters of four, reordered
taken as written, split to hold the other piece

explanation.surface: Look for a group of four people somewhere in an ancient marketplace.
explanation.definitionFit: The forum was the public square and market-place of an ancient Roman town.

clue.text: Oil-man opposed to meeting

blocks.note: the definition: a word that names both a fragrant oil and a man
the mirror instruction: a short word turned against itself and joined to its own reflection

explanation.surface: An oil executive who refuses to attend a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opposed' is read as facing the other way: a word set against its own mirror image, so the answer reads the same in both directions.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is another name for attar, the oil of roses, and Otto is also a man's name.

clue.text: Area between Indian and Pacific Oceans with variation in sea-tides

definitions.text: Area between Indian and Pacific Oceans

indicators.note: a variation is a changed version, so the letters following take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, hyphen dropped

explanation.surface: A geography note on the shifting tides of the seas between two oceans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a connecting word, but it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: The East Indies is the old name for the island archipelago of South-East Asia, lying between those two oceans.

clue.text: Concerned with tender ties

blocks.note: first meaning: involved or caring about something
second meaning: having a financial stake, tender being money and ties being the bonds it creates

explanation.walkthrough: 'tender ties' suggests affection; read it as money (legal tender) giving someone a stake.
explanation.definitionFit: An interested party is one with a stake, often financial, in an affair, and the word also means caring or involved.

clue.text: He arranges for girl to take crusty port

indicators.note: crusty means gruff and rough-tempered, suggesting the next word has been knocked about

blocks.note: a girl's name
the letters of port, rearranged

explanation.surface: A host arranges for a young woman to try a vintage port that has thrown a crust.
explanation.walkthrough: Crusted port really is a wine with a sediment, so 'crusty port' reads as a drink, not an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: An adaptor reworks a piece, such as a novel or tune, into a new form, so he arranges it.

clue.text: Bird with no revulsion for cheese

indicators.note: revulsion literally means a pulling back, so the word beside it is turned round

blocks.note: the stilt is a long-legged wading bird
taken as written before being turned

explanation.surface: A bird that has no disgust for cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revulsion' sounds like disgust; here it is read in its root sense of pulling back.
explanation.definitionFit: Stilton is a blue-veined English cheese.

clue.text: She once influenced greatly a measure on printed literature

blocks.note: an em is a printer's unit of width
the press is printed newspapers and journals

explanation.surface: A woman of the past whose sway over the printed word was great.
explanation.definitionFit: An empress was a female ruler, a woman who held great power over an empire.

clue.text: Moon-starer

blocks.note: the whole clue doubles as the letters to rework

explanation.walkthrough: There is no signal word: the clue is both a description of the answer and an exact rearrangement of it, a famous old anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronomer studies the heavens, and gazing at the moon is part of that work.

clue.text: Verbal inconsistency in the edict

blocks.note: first meaning: an Irish ..., a self-contradictory statement
second meaning: a formal decree issued by the Pope

explanation.surface: Someone spots a contradiction in the wording of an official decree.
explanation.definitionFit: An Irish bull is a ludicrously self-contradictory remark, and a papal bull is a formal decree.

clue.text: Feign sickness in attempt to nail germ

indicators.note: an attempt is a try at making something, so the words following are only a rough first go at the right order

blocks.note: taken as written: eight letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A shirker pretends to be ill while trying to pin down a bug.
explanation.definitionFit: To malinger is to pretend to be ill to avoid work or duty.

clue.text: Writer in feigned ignorance of his upbringing?

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning a gap between them
in a down clue, bringing something up means reading it from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: the last two letters of feigned and the first two of ignorance, run together

explanation.surface: An author pretends not to know how he was brought up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upbringing' looks like a reference to childhood; in a down clue it means the hidden letters are read upwards. André Gide was a French novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: André Gide was a French novelist and Nobel laureate, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Black mark for bringing pornography to church

blocks.note: smut is indecent material
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A churchgoer earns disgrace for bringing dirty magazines to the service.
explanation.definitionFit: A smutch is a dirty smudge or stain, a sooty black mark.

clue.text: Went up like fish?

blocks.note: first meaning: climbed, as a wall or cliff
second meaning: covered in scales, as a fish's skin is

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'fish' are not climbing anything: the second half is a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: To scale is to climb, and a scaled creature, like a fish, has a covering of small plates.

clue.text: American traffic controller proceeds to sacrifice redhead for the sake of quiet

indicators.note: sacrificing one thing is giving it up in exchange for something else, a swap
for the sake of names what is gained in return for the thing given up

blocks.note: taken as written
the head, or first letter, of red goes out
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, quiet

explanation.surface: A US traffic officer gives up a red-haired colleague to keep things calm.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping the R for P turns the letters of 'proceeds' into those of the answer, but the clue gives no signal to rearrange them; that step is left unmarked.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed cop is informal American English for a traffic police officer who catches speeding drivers.
